## Topshe: a local browser model, with clear boundaries

URL: https://saswatasg.com/blog/topshe-browser-voice-ai

Building a browser-local language-model experiment, while separating model privacy from speech APIs and planned integrations.

Topshe is a personal assistant experiment with language model inference in the browser. That is a specific technical boundary: it does not mean every speech feature is offline, every browser is supported, or every planned integration is already implemented. Start with a bounded experiment The product question is whether a small local model can make an assistant useful without routing every conversation through a hosted language model API. Topshe uses a quantised Qwen 2.5 model through wllama and WebAssembly, with a React interface and local conversation storage. The name comes from Feluda’s assistant in Satyajit Ray’s stories. In product terms, the intended role is similarly modest: help with a question or a small planning task. It remains an experiment, not a promise that a small browser model can replace a complete connected assistant. Local inference has a first use cost The documented model download is approximately 900 MB. That makes first use readiness a separate experience from later conversations. A progress state, recoverable downloads and an honest explanation of device requirements matter more than calling the product frictionless. Running inference locally also moves constraints onto the user’s device. Available memory, browser behavior and competing activity can affect the experience. There is no published representative device benchmark establishing a universal response time claim, so this case does not invent one. Separate the voice pipeline from the model The project uses browser speech APIs for recognition and synthesis. A browser can process speech differently from how the language model processes text. In particular, speech recognition may involve a remote service. A locally running model is therefore insufficient evidence for a claim that no data leaves the device. Wake word support uses Picovoice Porcupine and requires its own access key. Push to talk is a fallback. These are product dependencies, not details to hide behind a broad offline label. The MDN SpeechRecognition documentation https://developer.mozilla.org/en US/docs/Web/API/SpeechRecognition explains the browser support and remote processing caveats. Delivered scope versus future ambition The repository documents local conversation history with IndexedDB and an offline capable application shell. It also describes calendar, email, news and smart home integrations as planned. Those ideas should be read as a roadmap, not features a visitor can already rely on. WebGPU is not an established completed acceleration path in the documented implementation. Likewise, a compatibility statement in a README is not a substitute for a tested device matrix. Text only fallbacks and clear unavailable states are part of making the current scope understandable. The next useful evidence Before positioning this as a dependable assistant, I would want first use completion rates, model load failures, memory use and response latency across representative devices. Speech should be evaluated separately, with its permissions and processing path made visible. Integration tests should follow actual connected workflows as they are built. These are future validation needs, not results claimed from this project. The current artifact demonstrates browser local inference and the interface around it. The lesson is to make a narrow privacy claim accurately, and to treat dependencies and unsupported capabilities as part of the user experience. See the Topshe implementation and roadmap https://github.com/saswatasg/topshe for the documented architecture and current scope.

## TGB Hunt: outreach workflows and automation limits

URL: https://saswatasg.com/blog/tgb-hunt-linkedin-outreach-agent

A self-hosted outreach experiment: task orchestration, campaign state and the limits of automated platform actions.

TGB Hunt is a self hosted Django and Playwright outreach experiment. Its useful engineering story is campaign tasks, state tracking and follow up orchestration. Its implementation can send automatically; it should not be described as a system where every message always receives human approval. The workflow behind the interface Outreach is a sequence of states rather than a single text generation task. A campaign needs to know what has been attempted, what remains pending, which connection requests have changed status and whether a follow up should be scheduled. Losing those distinctions can create duplicate or badly timed actions. The repository includes task handlers for connections, follow ups and pending request checks, alongside campaign records and background execution. Django provides the application and persistence layer; Playwright operates the browser. The language model participates in the workflow, but the product is not simply a prompt wrapped in a button. State is a product requirement A useful task record should distinguish intended work from attempted work and confirmed completion. Browser activity can fail in ways that are not equivalent: navigation may fail before an action, an action may complete before confirmation is recorded, or a platform state may change between checks. The project includes reconciliation and failed state handling. Those mechanisms are important implementation artifacts. They do not establish that every edge case is covered or that the platform will continue to accept the same interaction behavior. A reliable claim needs reproducible tests and operational evidence, not only the presence of task code. Correcting the approval claim The public connection task handler can perform the send action. The implementation reviewed here does not establish a mandatory human decision before each individual send. The earlier portfolio description of an always reviewed drafting agent overstated that boundary. A review first workflow would be a meaningful future product change: persist a proposed action, display its recipient and content, obtain approval, then execute and record the result. That is a recommendation, not an existing capability being claimed here. Platform constraints shape the product An external platform is more than a browser surface. Its policies, account permissions and interface changes constrain what a product can responsibly offer. LinkedIn documents restrictions around prohibited software and automated activity in its official help guidance https://www.linkedin.com/help/linkedin/answer/a1341387 . This project should therefore remain an archived technical experiment rather than a promise of dependable recruiter outreach. The portfolio does not claim policy compliance, zero account risk, universal compatibility or an unattended service guarantee. Those would require evidence beyond a working browser task. What is and is not measured There is no traceable public dataset supporting the earlier reply rate, approval rate or meeting claims. This revised note removes them. Repository history and release counts show development activity; they are not proof of user value or conversion improvement. A stronger future evaluation would measure task state correctness, duplicate prevention, recovery behavior and the distinction between drafted and executed actions. Any user outcome study would also need a defined sample, time window and attribution method. Until then, the defensible contribution is workflow engineering and an explicit account of its limitations. The TGB Hunt repository https://github.com/saswatasg/TGBhunt contains the implementation. It is presented here as an archive, with no invented business result.

## DhanPlan: monthly planning with visible assumptions

URL: https://saswatasg.com/blog/dhanplan-retirement-calculator

How DhanPlan connects Indian savings instruments, retirement withdrawals, gap-solving and stress scenarios in a versioned monthly model.

DhanPlan is an India focused retirement planning product. The current story is a monthly model connecting savings, assets and retirement withdrawals, with assumptions and limitations made visible. A projection is a scenario, not a guarantee or proof of financial model accuracy. A plan needs more than a final number A retirement target is useful only when someone can understand the path to it. Contributions occur over time, different instruments have different rules, assets may mature at different points and spending continues after retirement. A single compound growth figure cannot explain all of those interactions. DhanPlan’s product direction is to connect those elements in one plan. The interface needs to communicate which inputs drive the result and which changes are meaningful. Showing a large future corpus without explaining inflation or withdrawals would make the output easier to misread. Model the sequence month by month The published methodology for Engine 2.0.0 describes a monthly ledger with contributions, balances, instrument behavior and retirement withdrawals. The rules review date is 2 October 2026. Instruments include EPF, PPF, NPS, deposits, precious metals and property related cash flows alongside investment assumptions. The point of a shared ledger is consistency across the plan. A maturity event after retirement still matters; an asset should not silently disappear because it falls outside the contribution phase. Versioning also gives a correction a visible context instead of presenting every output as timeless truth. Make the gap actionable The gap solving feature reruns the model to explore the contribution change needed under the selected assumptions. It is different from promising that a particular investment will achieve the target. It depends on the same return, inflation, timing and cash flow choices as the underlying projection. Nominal and inflation adjusted views answer different questions. The former describes future currency amounts; the latter helps a person think about purchasing power. An understandable product keeps that distinction visible rather than switching between them without explanation. Stress the assumptions, not just the interface The documented stress scenarios include higher and lower assumptions and 1,000 Monte Carlo paths. These show how sensitive a plan can be to the selected inputs. Simulated paths are conditional on their modelling assumptions; they are not a complete picture of every possible future event. A helpful experience should let a user see which assumption changed and how the result moved. It should also explain when a feature is a deterministic calculation and when it is a simulated distribution. More scenarios are not automatically better if their meaning is hard to understand. Keep limitations beside the model The methodology documents limits around fees, exit costs, some tax timing and other instrument or household details. A calculator cannot infer every future household decision from a short form. The product should make exclusions discoverable and date sensitive rules traceable to the methodology. This portfolio does not claim independently verified financial accuracy, a fabricated test count or measured adoption. Those claims would need their own evidence. The delivered artifact is a live planning interface and a documented model; further verification should use reconciled fixtures and reproducible scenarios. The broader product lesson is to treat assumptions as part of the interface. A user should be able to inspect what a number means, change its inputs and understand where the model stops. See DhanPlan https://www.dhanplan.in/ and its current methodology https://www.dhanplan.in/methodology for the versioned rules and limitations.

## AI image greetings lifted feature engagement by 168%

URL: https://saswatasg.com/blog/ai-send-greetings-168

A dormant 'Send Greetings' feature, an image-gen model, and a festival calendar across 27 occasions — feature engagement up 168% at LiveKeeping.

At LiveKeeping, I worked on an AI image generation integration for the Pro+ Send Greetings feature and a geo segmented calendar of 27 occasions across five regional groupings. The supplied record reports +168% feature engagement; it does not establish the same increase in overall product retention or revenue. Give the feature a relevant moment The feature helps a merchant create greetings for customers. Its product challenge is broader than generating an attractive image: the occasion, language and business context need to make the greeting useful at the moment someone wants to send it. The documented work combines image generation with a regional festival calendar. This gives the product a structured source of relevant occasions rather than treating every user as if they follow the same national calendar. Five groupings provide a practical segmentation basis; they are not a claim to represent every local custom. Make the integration understandable The supplied work describes the Nano Banana image model integration and its role in producing greeting artwork. The product flow brings together the selected occasion, business context and image generation. A user needs to understand what will be created and have a clear path to review the result. An AI integration should be assessed through the task it helps complete. Generation availability alone does not show that someone created a usable card or sent it successfully. Those steps deserve separate instrumentation rather than one undifferentiated AI use counter. Calendar design is part of the product The 27 occasion calendar makes timing and relevance explicit. Regional mapping connects the schedule to the merchant’s context. The feature work also fits the broader lifecycle messaging architecture, where priority, daily limits and conflicting messages need to be considered. A useful notification is a prompt for a relevant task. Sending more reminders is not automatically better, and the calendar should not be interpreted as permission to contact every merchant for every occasion. The design needs a path from relevance to action, alongside controls for message fatigue. What the reported result means The supplied record reports a 168% improvement in feature engagement. The public evidence does not provide the underlying event definition, denominator, cohort dates or attribution method. This case therefore keeps the label at feature engagement, rather than presenting it as an increase in DAU, revenue, retention or cards per user. The earlier article included unsupported claims about eighteen months of usage, cards per active user, cache hit rates and evergreen volume share. Those figures are not needed to explain the contribution and have been removed. A defensible result should survive without invented supporting precision. What I would measure next The next evidence pack should define the engaged action and comparison period, then separate generation attempts, successful images, user edits and completed sends. Regional uptake and repeat use would help distinguish one time curiosity from recurring usefulness. These are measurement questions, not results claimed here. The delivered story is a feature integration and a structured occasion calendar, with a reported engagement outcome whose measurement scope remains limited in the public case. Read the Send Greetings case /case studies/livekeeping send greetings alongside the notification architecture /blog/push notification architecture . Google's Gemini image generation documentation https://ai.google.dev/gemini api/docs/image generation provides the model context; it does not validate this product's engagement result.

## The 17:1 e-way bill gap: diagnosing B2B adoption

URL: https://saswatasg.com/blog/e-invoice-adoption-gap

A workflow investigation at LiveKeeping identified 17:1 and 19:1 adoption gaps and informed executive product discussions.

At LiveKeeping, investigating native compliance feature usage revealed a 17:1 E Way Bill gap and a 19:1 E Invoice gap relative to external Tally origin workflows. The work informed executive roadmap discussions. It does not establish a shipped connector or measured recovery in adoption. Ask where the work already happens A feature can be available to a paying customer without becoming their preferred workflow. For an accounting product, the surrounding system matters: invoices, bookkeeping and compliance activities are connected. Looking only at the native feature funnel can miss the substitute workflow a customer already uses. My work combined analysis of API transactions, product usage and workflow context. The purpose was to understand why users with access to native modules were still generating compliance documents elsewhere. This is a product discovery problem before it is a feature redesign problem. Keep the ratios tied to their scope The supplied work record reports a 17:1 E Way Bill gap and a 19:1 E Invoice gap, comparing external and native activity. These ratios describe the investigated usage context; they are not a market wide share estimate or proof that seventeen times as many distinct customers rejected the product. The underlying cohort table, time window and denominator are not reproduced publicly here. That limits how far a reader should generalize the result. A stronger evidence pack would show the qualifying subscriber cohort, event definitions, comparison period and treatment of repeated transactions. Translate the finding into a decision The analysis was presented at VP and CEO level and contributed to the roadmap discussion. The important change was the framing: low feature usage needed to be understood alongside the workflow customers were already completing outside the native interface. A connector, data transfer change or revised entry point could be options to investigate. This case does not assert that a particular middleware implementation was built, installed by 50,000 merchants or achieved a latency target. Those were unsupported additions in the earlier article and have been removed. Separate adoption from reliability A parallel workstream analysed 100K+ API transaction logs and addressed compliance journey errors. The supplied record reports a 58% reduction in rejection rate for that reliability work. This is a different measure from adoption: fewer rejected submissions do not establish that users moved their workflow into the native module. Keeping those results separate makes the case more useful. One stream asks why customers use another path; the other asks what fails when a compliance transaction is attempted. They may influence the same roadmap, but their outcomes should not be added together or treated as evidence of the same intervention. What the public case establishes The defensible contribution is analysis, problem framing and an executive narrative connecting feature usage to real workflows. It also shows the importance of distinguishing a diagnostic finding from a delivered solution. Further rollout claims would require release records, cohort adoption data and a measurement window. For the product context, see the official E Way Bill portal https://ewaybillgst.gov.in/ and the full compliance discovery case /case studies/livekeeping compliance gap . The lesson is to measure the work customers are completing, not simply the interface they are declining to use.

## Discovery that continues into solution delivery

URL: https://saswatasg.com/blog/discovery-to-roadmap

Building discovery at Upcore Technologies: structured research, opportunity prioritization and end-to-end solution delivery ownership for 23+ clients.

At Upcore Technologies, I built the discovery practice and derived solutions while managing their delivery end to end for 23+ clients. Structured conversations, a 500+ response survey and an evidence framework supported prioritization. The work connects problem understanding to solution definition and delivery ownership. Enterprise interest in AI is broad. A useful product direction needs a more concrete starting point: a workflow, a constraint and a reason to change it. Discovery helps define that starting point. Delivery tests whether the proposed solution can become something the client can use. What I worked on I built the discovery practice from scratch, including structured client conversations, a survey with 500+ respondents and a framework for organizing evidence into priorities. The work also included 20+ prospective client conversations across 12 verticals and a top three opportunity brief. Those counts describe research scope. They are not a combined sample, and the brief is a prioritization output rather than evidence that three products launched. Alongside discovery, I derived solutions and managed their delivery end to end for 23+ clients. I coordinated sprint planning and backlogs with a six developer team, without formal reporting authority. What the evidence needs to explain An interview count is useful context, but it does not explain a product decision by itself. A decision needs the problem, the evidence supporting it, the alternatives and the constraints. The following is a practical checklist for reviewing an opportunity brief—not a reproduction of a particular interview script or a confidential client artifact: Problem: Which workflow is difficult, and for whom? Evidence: What was observed directly, and what remains an assumption? Value: What changes if the problem is solved? Feasibility: What data, integration or operational constraints matter? Next step: What should be investigated, demonstrated or delivered next? The distinction between evidence and assumption matters throughout the process. A stated interest is different from budget approval. A positive demo reaction is different from production acceptance. A forecast is different from realized revenue. Carrying the solution into delivery Discovery and delivery belong in the same professional story because a proposed solution still needs definition and execution. My Upcore work includes both deriving solutions and managing their delivery for 23+ clients. Inventory Leveling & Procurement Intelligence /case studies/upcore inventory leveling is a public artifact within that work. The client demo connects orders, component requirements, stock and lead times to procurement planning. Its interface and calculation tests make the solution inspectable. The public repository and test documentation https://github.com/saswatasg/inventory leveling agent describe the implementation. It uses mock data and has no live ERP integration. That is its delivery stage, not a weakness to hide or a production outcome to invent. The artifact demonstrates a workflow and validated calculations; deployment and business impact require additional evidence. Measure the right kind of result For this work, three categories should remain distinct: Category What it establishes Research Scope, evidence and prioritization outputs Client delivery Responsibility for defining and carrying solutions through delivery Business impact Measured changes with a baseline, window and attribution A strong case study connects these categories where the evidence supports it. Its strongest evidence is the decision trail: what changed, why it changed and what the team delivered. Read the discovery and solution delivery overview /case studies/upcore discovery for the role and scope, or the qualification framework /case studies/upcore lead scoring for a separate example of turning information into an operational decision.

## FilmRisk.AI: what a weak backtest changed

URL: https://saswatasg.com/blog/film-risk-engine

A film-risk experiment with temporal validation, weak baseline comparisons and explicit data limits. What the evaluation changed.

FilmRisk.AI explores whether public film data can support a pre release risk score. The published evaluation did not establish a useful predictive advantage. That finding changes how the project should be presented: as an evaluation experiment, rather than a successful greenlight decision engine. The product question A score is only useful if it improves the decision someone could make without it. For a film risk product, an attractive interface or a complicated model does not establish that improvement. The relevant question is whether the prediction adds reliable information before release, using inputs available at that time. The project combines a gradient boosted model with empirical Bayesian priors and a component based scoring approach. Its implementation is in TypeScript with a Next.js interface. Simulation can describe uncertainty under assumptions, but it cannot repair missing data or prove that a score is commercially useful. Data coverage is part of the result The repository documents 2,454 film records spanning 2001–2025. Only 729 have the financial information required for training. This is not a representative financial history of every film in the period. It is a subset shaped by which figures were publicly reported and could be assembled. That missingness creates a practical constraint: the product must not imply that a score describes the whole industry equally well. Dataset size, the training subset and the population a model can reasonably speak about are different things. Test on later films, not shuffled familiarity The published primary evaluation uses 14 rolling annual folds with 658 tested films. This temporal approach asks whether knowledge from earlier releases helps with later releases. It is more relevant to a pre release decision than simply demonstrating a fit to familiar records. Outcome derived concept features were removed from the evaluation to address leakage. User supplied pre release concept inputs in the product are not thereby validated by that historical test. The distinction matters because the implemented interface and the tested prediction path need not be identical. What the benchmark actually says The published results report 29.3% classification accuracy, compared with 63.7% for a band median baseline and 80.5% for an always flop baseline. Greenlight precision was 11.3%, against a base hit rate of 11.0%. Reported RMSE was 1.303, compared with 1.23 for the band median baseline. These metrics answer different questions; they should not be collapsed into a single success percentage. In particular, high accuracy from predicting a dominant class is not a useful recommendation system. Conversely, these results do not justify marketing the more complex model as superior. They are published repository results, not an independently reproduced evaluation in this portfolio audit. What I would require before expanding it The next work should improve provenance, establish a decision relevant baseline and test the exact inputs used before release. A larger interface or more model components should follow evidence of usefulness, rather than substitute for it. A small recent holdout also needs its sample size made visible. The portfolio value here is the willingness to expose an unfavorable result and change the claim. This remains a research experiment. It should not be used as a validated financial decision tool. The implementation, benchmark and limitations are available in the FilmRisk.AI repository https://github.com/saswatasg/FilmRisk.AI and its published benchmark results https://github.com/saswatasg/FilmRisk.AI/blob/main/src/generated/benchmark results.json .

## Lead routing: observed signals and explicit pilot targets

URL: https://saswatasg.com/blog/lead-routing-gold-silver-bronze

Designing a tiered lead-allocation system at Sierra Living Concepts, separating observed source performance from pilot targets.

At Sierra Living Concepts, I designed a Gold/Silver/Bronze lead allocation system using source performance, agent capacity and escalation rules. The observed conversion data informed the design. The target of 5.2 to 3.5 days to close is a pilot objective, not a demonstrated result. The decision behind the queue The work addressed how a four agent team should allocate leads arriving from six sources. Giving every source the same handling path ignores differences in intent and conversion. A useful routing system needs to translate those differences into a next action without making the source label permanent. The available analysis reports website form conversion at 63.5%, chat at 4.7% and cart abandonment leads at 0.4%. These are observed source rates in the analysed dataset. They do not establish a universal probability of closing the next individual lead, and low volume categories need particular care. Three tiers, different handling Gold prioritizes high intent sources for specialist attention. Silver provides a structured follow up path for intermediate intent. Bronze reduces repetitive manual handling while retaining a route to human review when stronger intent appears. The important product choice is to make the next action clear. A tier alone is not enough: the team needs assignment rules, capacity handling and escalation conditions. A response indicating a substantial custom order can justify reconsidering a low initial priority. This is operational decision logic, not a learned model being claimed to predict every outcome. Capacity changes the routing decision Availability and agent specialization matter alongside source performance. The allocation design considered day by day coverage and a specialist path for high intent enquiries. Those rules should be evaluated against both response delay and conversion; waiting for a specialist is not automatically better than a prompt response. The earlier article claimed a measured 25% advantage from delaying a particular day's leads. That comparison is not supported by the supplied record. It has been removed rather than generalized into advice. The Salesforce guide to lead management https://www.salesforce.com/sales/lead management/ provides broader process context, not validation of this case's results. Targets are not outcomes The supplied case describes a 30 day pilot progressing toward rollout. The design included targets for routing accuracy, automation coverage, specialist lead allocation and reducing days to close from 5.2 to 3.5. A target remains a target until a comparable post change measurement is available. The earlier portfolio presented 90% routing accuracy, 90% chat automation and increased daily specialist leads as achieved results. This revision treats them as pilot objectives. It also removes a dollar saving estimate presented as if the money had been recovered. Expected conversion revenue is a scenario, not realized savings. The evidence that would close the loop A stronger follow up would report assignment compliance, response time, escalation errors and conversion by source and handler over a defined period. Lead quality and seasonal changes need to be accounted for when comparing before and after. The team also needs to know whether the system improved workload balance rather than only moving one metric. This case establishes an allocation design grounded in observed source differences, with an explicit measurement plan. It does not claim a causal increase in revenue or a verified reduction in days to close. See the full lead allocation case /case studies/sierra lead allocation for the routing and pilot structure.

## How a form fix lifted lead submissions by 124% in 28 days

URL: https://saswatasg.com/blog/lead-form-overhaul-124

A field-by-field form teardown with GA4 events and Clarity — one restrictive field caused 23% of drop-offs. The fix raised submissions +124% in 28 days.

Lead forms leak at one field, not from length. A hidden phone format rule drove 23% of drop offs. Mask + inline validation + intent labels lifted submissions 124% in 28 days — with more fields, not fewer. The marketing ask was the sane one: more traffic . The team wanted a bigger top of funnel. The data said we'd been paying for traffic and then spilling a big slice of it on the walk to the callback — a form with a 23% leak at one field is a bigger lever than any ad budget increase. But I had to prove the leak existed before I could ask for the fix. A completion rate was not enough The problem was that an aggregate completion rate was the only thing the team could see — one number, and several theories about what to do with it. Measurement scope: this rebuild reports +124% lead submissions in 28 days. The separate role level record of 2.14% → 4.40% represents approximately +105%. The available records do not establish the same window or denominator; these figures should not be treated as consecutive stages of one experiment. The theories were the enemy. "It's too long." The form wasn't long, but the phrase had staying power. "The latency is bad." True — client side fields took 3–5 seconds to initialize on typical connections. "The labels are confusing." Also plausible — but nobody could prove it. Every one of those was a snipe at the aggregate. A real diagnosis needs to know: at which exact field does the flow die? Field by field instrumentation — the recipe Same play as the checkout, two levels down. Where the checkout got an event per step, this got an event per field: GA4 custom events per interaction — field focus, first touch, error, submit attempt. Microsoft Clarity recordings + binge click heatmaps — 50+ complete form sessions across desktop and mobile. A field by field funnel built from first touch to final submit. The funnel is the entire product. Without it you can't even name the leak — with it you can walk up to a designer and point at a phone input on a Monday afternoon. The moment the layout turned One pattern appeared in every single session. Users reached the phone field, typed, got nothing — and left. The culprit was a phone number format check expecting +1 555 000 0000 , on a desktop keyboard, failing if the input didn't match exactly . No hint. No formatting. No inline feedback. Type a digit the parser didn't like and the field stayed red — if it gave any signal at all. Then the tab closes. 23% of all abandonment, from one restriction — more than double the next worst field. The team had spent weeks guessing "too long." The sessions said "the phone field." The three fixes we shipped plus the real one Fix What we did Why it worked Format hint Visible masked input + placeholder before the first touch Users learned the expected format without an error Inline validation Accept the moment the input becomes valid Errors never wait for a submit failure Contextual microcopy Case specific labels "Work phone" vs "Any phone" Users understood intent instead of bouncing But the deeper fix wasn't a field fix. The form shipped to every visitor with one shape, and shape was part of the leak too. We rebuilt it into category specific modules Material 3 https://m3.material.io/ components + the latency cuts so a Custom Furniture visitor got the exact fields a custom quote visitor needs. Same form, different face, zero extra load. The numbers Metric Before After Lead submissions baseline +124% Mobile completion time baseline −41% Rage clicks baseline −68% Why the fix worked — and why "shorter form" never would have The hard part of this project was that every instinct pointed the wrong way. "Shorten the form" is the classic advice, and it's usually wrong — here's why we know: The leak wasn't length. Users reached the phone field — deep in the form — and left there. Shortening wouldn't have removed the field that mattered; it would just have moved the leak closer to the top. Latency set the tone. Client side fields took 3–5 seconds to initialize on typical connections. On mobile that felt like the form was broken before the user even looked at it. Fast initialization quietly removed the "this is slow, this is broken" walk away before a user ever typed. Expectation beats both. A user who can see the required format in a placeholder, and gets live "yes, that's right" feedback the moment it's valid, doesn't need to error at all. The form stopped producing rejection moments. That last point is the one worth stealing. Good form design is mostly removing the moment of rejection. Every field that can be validated inline should be — web.dev's form best practices https://web.dev/learn/forms cover the mechanics. Every format that can be shown ahead of typing should be. If you never show a user a red field, you never give them a reason to walk away. What changes when you ship this on mobile the real test Desktop was the easy half. On mobile it was stark: The phone field popped a numeric keypad that had no digit formatted guide — users were guessing the mask the parser wanted. Form width and focus states didn't match the brand's storefront; the form read as "generic template," not part of the site. Submission after latency was worse on mobile than desktop — and the rage click on a dead field meant that user never came back. The module rework bundled mobile specific copy and the Material 3 components. The −41% mobile completion time metric you see in the table came largely from the field logic , not the CSS. Why this was defensible in a room of skeptics The move that made this easy to defend: field level funnels make the fix ownable . When a designer asked "prove the phone field was it," the answer wasn't a theory — it was a row in a table and 30 seconds of shared Clarity playback. Every form project should be presented that way: as a ladder with one rung shown red, and the fix mapped to the exact rung. The full field by field detail lives at the lead form case study /case studies/lead form . If your form leaks and you don't know why, this month 1. Install field level events — focus, error, submit. Run two weeks, export the funnel. 2. Watch three real mobile sessions. You'll see the leak in one lunch break. 3. Remove the rejections, not the length. Placeholder masks, inline validation, specific microcopy. Ship, then re measure the same funnel. What I'd do differently Instrument before you guess. We burned a week on "the form is too long" because it was a pleasant hypothesis. The field level events were built in week two, and they'd have saved us the week. Watch three real mobile sessions early. Two weeks of Clarity told us more than three months of dashboards — because a dashboard can't show a phone input failing in silence. Full spec and code adjacent details: the lead form case study /case studies/lead form . And if you've read the checkout teardown — the same measure before you fix play at a different scale — this is the field level version: checkout abandonment /blog/checkout abandonment 73 to 54 .

## The cheapest e-commerce CRO: ship one fix a week

URL: https://saswatasg.com/blog/one-fix-a-week-cro

17 boring fixes beat one big redesign. Weekly micro-forensics on checkout, forms and search — each measured — compound faster than a quarterly splash.

CRO on a D2C furniture brand wasn't a redesign — it was weekly micro forensics with a metric attached to each decision. Fix the checkout surprise, fix the form field, fix the search weights, and measure each. One measured fix a week compounds faster and with less risk than one big bang redesign a quarter. Everyone on the team wanted the splashy redesign. Nobody wanted the 17 boring fixes. The splashy redesign was a bet on taste; the boring fixes were a bet on measurement — and measurement is the only thing that pays out predictably. Baymard's research https://baymard.com/lists/cart abandonment rate puts average cart abandonment near 70% — which means every store is sitting on a backlog of small, findable leaks that no single redesign will ever name. What "one fix a week" meant at Sierra We flattened CRO into a repeatable pipeline, four steps, no heroics involved: 1. Pick a funnel step — checkout, form, search, or product page. 2. Form a short hypothesis from events + sessions, in one sentence. 3. Ship the cheapest change that tests it — not the most impressive one. 4. Watch one KPI for two weeks. Keep it, kill it, or learn from it. No orphan changes. The whole discipline is step 4. A fix that isn't watched is a guess with a build ticket attached. A sample of fixes that shipped Shipping on the cart page. Surprise shipping cost was killing checkout; the display fix alone moved the abandonment needle /blog/checkout abandonment 73 to 54 . Search synonyms re weighting. Not flashy, but search attributed revenue lifted +14% — one of the store's quietest, highest ROI wins. Form field objection microcopy. One uncommunicated field was costing the team the form fix /blog/lead form overhaul 124 ; a label, not a field deletion, turned it around. The cadence vs the splash One fix a week The big redesign Learning per change high low Ramp smooth, reversible risky, all or nothing Attribution the change owns the delta noise Measurement rigorous loud but noisy The telling column is attribution. Redesigns can't tell you which thing worked. Weekly fixes can — because each one is small enough to name as the cause. What I'd do differently Keep a central hypothesis log. If a thought sits unmeasured for a week, it's dead. A queue of micro tests compounds like a good backlog. Attach every fix to one KPI. Vague fixes kill the funnel's red thread; a fix with an owner KPI survives review. When not to use the weekly cadence Being honest about the limits is part of the discipline. One fix a week fails in four situations: 1. The funnel is structurally broken. If your checkout errors on half of attempts regardless of UX, fixing the copy is grinding powder. Fix the architecture once, deeply. 2. You don't have measurement. The cadence is the measurement. Without events, the weekly fix is a prayer. Instrument first or skip the routine. 3. The win can't be isolated. Some changes entangle — new page + new template + new flow in one PR. The cadence requires one change per KPI. Resist combos. 4. The team reuses "the splash always fails" as an excuse for slowness. A weekly fix that never ships is just a slow redesign with braver language. The cadence has to ship. Knowing the four exit conditions is what separates a shop that does CRO from a shop that talks about it. How to read the two week window A common question when teams adopt this: "what if the KPI hasn't moved after two weeks?" Three honest answers, in order of likelihood: The fix doesn't matter most common . It moved nothing; kill it, log it, move on. Not every change needs to win. The KPI is too coarse. If the window can't show the delta, refine the KPI before re running. You need a variant, not a removal. If the data hints the direction was right but the execution weak, run the next cheap variant — don't abandon the line. The trap is leaving the window open forever. A fix that "might still pay off next month" is a fix that's never been measured. Close the loop on schedule; keep the learnings in the log. The compounding math, plainly Rough numbers, no spreadsheet glamour: one fix at a rough 1–5% lift per test — realistically optimistic — compounds into something a single redesign can't match. But you shouldn't believe me: the actual people reading this post have the checkout −26% , the form +124% , and the category +34% qualified as the evidence trail from a single disciplined year. That's the whole pitch of the weekly cadence. It's unglamorous, and it pays predictably. The mechanics behind those fixes are the connected stories: the category redesign /blog/category page redesign plus34 , the form teardown /blog/lead form overhaul 124 , and the flagship checkout story /blog/checkout abandonment 73 to 54 — with the full numbers in the cart & checkout case study /case studies/cart checkout . Read them together — they're the same discipline at three different scales. The one fix cadence, run for real Here's what a surrogate month of the routine looked like on a D2C store — not a master plan, just four Tuesdays: Week 1 fix: Shipping shown on cart page. Hypothesis: users bail at the shipping step because the total arrives late. KPI: checkout abandonment. Result: the needle moved; keep. Week 2 fix: Promo field validation. Hypothesis: rage clicks came from a field that ate input without a reply. KPI: rage clicks at the field. Result: cleaned up 68% of them; keep already covered in the form post /blog/lead form overhaul 124 . Week 3 fix: Search synonym weights. Hypothesis: searchers didn't find "buffet" because weights skewed "cabinet." KPI: search attributed revenue. Result: +14%, keep. Week 4 fix: Category page intent filter. Hypothesis: attribute filters ignore needs. KPI: qualified leads. Result: +34%, keep — covered in category /blog/category page redesign plus34 . That's the entire emotional experience of CRO at scale: boring change, boring measurement, boring win, repeated. The splash comes from compounding, not from any single Thursday. Why the boring framing is a superpower When you tell a stakeholder "we'll ship the smallest thing that could work," you're actually buying three things at once: 1. Faster learning — a one file change ships this week, not next quarter. 2. Reversibility — if it fails, you remove it without a postmortem. 3. Attribution — one change = one KPI, so when it moves you know why. The redesign offers the thrill of scale and the torture of unblameable noise. The weekly fix offers none of the thrill and all of the accountability — which is why it compounds.

## The data deep-dive: 480K sessions to three real problems

URL: https://saswatasg.com/blog/data-deep-dive-method

The method behind the Sierra checkout teardown: instrument the funnel first, form ranked hypotheses second, never optimize an unmeasured funnel.

A deep dive that changes metrics has two phases. First, instrument the funnel until you can name each drop off. Second, form ranked hypotheses. At Sierra, 480K sessions became three fixable problems in two weeks — because we never diagnosed an aggregate, only a funnel. "Cart abandonment is too high." That sentence sat in our metrics review for months, and everyone nodded, and nothing moved — because an aggregate number is unanswerable. When we finally stepped through 480K sessions properly, "abandonment" turned out to be three completely different problems wearing one trench coat. The failure happens four steps before the diagnosis: no events, no recordings, no funnel, no ranked hypotheses — and then a hunch gets a roadmap slot. Phase 1 — Instrument the funnel You cannot fix a funnel you cannot step through. The deep dive starts with one ask: name every step. Install step level events on the surface you care about view → engage → convert or checkout view → shipping → payment → purchase Layer on session recordings: heatmaps, rage clicks, scroll depth Put the output in BigQuery so you can interrogate it, not just chart it Only when you can answer "which step loses the most, and which looks like a single cause" do conclusions become credible. The shape of the events An event per step pattern looks roughly like this — the exact fields vary by funnel, but the principle doesn't: Every step gets an event. No "checkout started" aggregate — you need the staircase. The Clarity setup Microsoft Clarity https://clarity.microsoft.com/ is free and unsampled, which matters more than any premium feature: Recordings on for 100% of sessions sampling kills the rare but critical paths Heatmaps on every checkout step URL Rage click detection on form fields, buttons, promo inputs Dead click mapping — clicks on non interactive elements reveal broken expectations The BigQuery schema Don't just chart in GA4. Stream the raw events to BigQuery via the GA4 BigQuery export https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/9358801 so you can interrogate them directly — a drop off by step query, segmented by device, looks roughly like this: SQL like this is the deep dive. The dashboard is the summary. Phase 2 — Ranked hypotheses Aggregate data lies politely; a funnel stops lying. Take the event tables and rank drop offs: Rank What you're testing 1 The step with the biggest unique loss 2 The step most likely to be one cause 3 The step that is easiest to measure after At Sierra this drill surfaced three distinct checkout problems — shipping surprise, promo rage click, payment dead end — that one aggregate percentage had been hiding. Each got an independent hypothesis, an independent fix, and an independent measurement window, so when the number moved we knew exactly which change owned it. The full breakdown — what each problem looked like in the session recordings, what shipped, and the before/after numbers 73.1% → 53.9% abandonment, +47% mobile CVR, +49% checkout completion — is in the checkout teardown /blog/checkout abandonment 73 to 54 . The rule that tells this apart from guesswork Two years of aggregate is weaker than two weeks of steps ; instrumentation expands signal, not volume. Cost estimates are hypotheses too. Just because a fix is one line doesn't make it the winner. Re read the funnel after shipping ; you only learn from the same instrument. Post mortem notes "Cart abandonment" was the trap; the funnel named three different things. Events are facts, recordings are opinions; trust the ones you can replay. Full mechanics in the checkout teardown /blog/checkout abandonment 73 to 54 . What I'd do differently I'd start recordings earlier — we had 480K sessions before our first replay window. I'd version the funnel definition like source code so "did the fix even change the view" is answerable in a ticket, not a debate. I'd build the hypothesis tracker before the first event — a simple sheet: hypothesis, owner, KPI, window, result. The template you can steal copy paste into Notion Hypothesis Owner KPI Window Evidence needed Result Decision one sentence, tied to a specific step name the one metric that proves it fixed, e.g. 2 weeks what the recording/event data must show fill after the window closes keep / kill / iterate Fill this before you write a single event. If you can't fill the "Evidence needed" column, you don't have a hypothesis — you have a hope. The anti patterns that kill deep dives 1. "Let's just add events and see what happens." No. Events without a question are noise. Write the hypothesis first. 2. "We'll A/B test the whole funnel." You can't attribute. Test one hypothesis per window. 3. "The dashboard says X." Dashboards aggregate. The deep dive disaggregates . If your dashboard and your deep dive agree, your deep dive failed. 4. "We don't have time for recordings." You don't have time not to. 50 sessions = 2 hours. The alternative is guessing for months. If your dashboard and your deep dive agree, your deep dive failed. The whole point of disaggregating is to find what the average was hiding. The same instrument first discipline is what found the single worst field in the lead form fix /blog/lead form overhaul 124 and the intent segmentation insight behind the category page redesign /blog/category page redesign plus34 — different funnels, same method. The full checkout numbers live in the cart & checkout case study /case studies/cart checkout .

## Daily report automation: 3 sources, 88 rows, 11 AM

URL: https://saswatasg.com/blog/daily-report-automation

A Google Apps Script pipeline unifying Kibana, MongoDB, and GA4 into one auto-populated report — what white-collar automation really costs.

Daily reporting is 90% ritual, 10% signal. For the team at LiveKeeping we built a Google Apps Script pipeline that unifies Kibana, MongoDB, and GA4 into one auto populated report — 88 mapped rows, delivered at 11 AM with zero manual steps. The automation wasn't the win; the agreed shape of the report was. Three tabs. One formula fight. One Slack paste. Thirty minutes, every morning, for whoever drew the short straw. Multiply by a working year and the "quick morning report" quietly costs a hundred plus hours nobody budgeted — invisible in product metrics, present every single day. We killed it in a week with Google Apps Script, and the code was the least interesting part. The pipeline Sources: Kibana compliance event logs , MongoDB user tier counts , Google Analytics 4 feature level engagement A Google Apps Script backend runs on a time driven trigger, pulls each source via APIs, and maps every row into one canonical schema Outputs: an auto populated Google Sheet at 11 AM before the morning sync The adapter pattern: how we made it survive API changes The first version had raw API calls sprinkled through the main script. When Kibana's Elasticsearch DSL changed, the whole pipeline broke. The fix: every source sits behind a tiny adapter — a single file with one contract: fetchData → normalized rows . When Kibana changes, you edit one file. The main orchestrator doesn't know Kibana exists — it just calls adapters.kibana.fetchData . The other adapters MongoDB adapter — uses the MongoDB Data API not a direct driver, since Apps Script can't hold connections : GA4 adapter — uses the GA4 Data API with a service account: The schema: 88 rows as a decision document Before any code, we sat down with the PM, the analyst, and the CTO and agreed on exactly what each row means . The schema doc: Row Metric Source Grain Owner 1–12 GST rejection errors by code Kibana Daily Compliance PM 13–18 User tier distribution MongoDB Daily Growth PM 19–30 Feature engagement Send Greetings, GST search, etc. GA4 Daily Feature PMs 31–88 Tier and region drill downs of the above All three Daily Shared The script just renders this agreement. When a stakeholder asks "why is row 23 that number?", the answer is in the schema doc, not the code. Error handling & monitoring what we learned the hard way The pipeline runs at 11 AM. If it fails, the team knows by 11:05. Here's how: Three failure modes we've hit: 1. Kibana token expiry — token lasts 24h; we added a refresh check before fetch 2. MongoDB Data API rate limit — 100 req/min; we batch the pipeline calls 3. GA4 quota exhaustion — the GA4 Data API https://developers.google.com/analytics/devguides/reporting/data/v1/quotas has daily token quotas; we cache the service account token for 1hr What made it stick and what snuck out The schema came first. We agreed on the 88 rows as a decision document before any script; the script just rendered the decision. Vendor lock in was the risk. Pipelines die when one API changes; each source sat behind a tiny adapter so a Kibana change = one file, not a rewrite. 0 manual steps. If a human must touch a pipeline daily, it will be touched differently by three humans. The result Metric Value Sources unified 3 Kibana, MongoDB, GA4 Rows mapped 88 canonical schema Delivery 11 AM daily, auto populated Manual steps 0 Team on call removed The cost breakdown what white collar automation really costs Cost item Monthly Notes Apps Script runtime $0 Free tier covers 6h/day; we use ~15min MongoDB Data API $0 Free tier 1M ops/month GA4 Data API $0 Free tier Slack webhook $0 Incoming webhook Engineering time build ~16 hrs One time Engineering time maintenance ~30 min/mo Token refresh, schema tweaks The "free" tier covers us completely — Apps Script quotas https://developers.google.com/apps script/guides/services/quotas allow far more runtime than a 15 minute daily job needs. The real cost is the design time — agreeing on the 88 rows took 3 meetings, 2 hours each. Automation doesn't remove the work. It removes the daily disagreement about what the work means. That's the part worth paying for. What I'd do differently Audit the output contract. I'd print the Sheet schema on a wall so users stopped asking "which tab is that again?" Version the pipeline. Apps Script projects drift; add a version marker the moment it becomes the team's firehose. Build the dry run mode earlier. A dry run flag that logs what would be written without writing it would've caught the Kibana schema drift a week earlier. Deep dive here: the daily report automation case study /case studies/livekeeping report automation . If you live in metrics heavy B2B, my compliance gap diagnostic /blog/e invoice adoption gap is home data hunting — the same habit of watching the numbers actually flow.

## 27 push notification triggers, 5 regions, one architecture

URL: https://saswatasg.com/blog/push-notification-architecture

Designing a notification system across renewals, transactional states, and conflict logic — with priority tiers and a daily cap users don't hate.

A push notification architecture decays into spam without a priority and cap system. We designed a lifecycle messaging system with 27+ triggers, P0–P3 priority tiers, a 3 slot daily cap, and 5 geo regions — for GST compliance software used by 50K+ Indian SMBs. The lesson: constrain volume so every send is earned. A GST rejection notice is worth a ₹10,000+ penalty if the merchant misses it. A "new feature " nudge is worth nothing if they don't. Send both the same afternoon and the merchant mutes you — and now your ₹10,000 alert dies in a muted channel next quarter. That's the real stakes of notification architecture: spam doesn't just annoy users, it destroys the channel you need for the messages that matter. This system's goal was to make every ping buy back its own attention, for a B2B SaaS with 50K+ SMBs and real money on the line. The 27+ trigger inventory We mapped the full lifecycle into four buckets: Renewal & billing — renewal reminders D 30, D 14, D 7, D 3, D 1 , trial expiry, invoice ready, payment failures, auto renewal confirmation Transactional states — ledger entry confirmed, GST return filed, payment received, reversal confirmed, credit note issued Conflicts & errors — GST rejection wrong GSTIN, mismatch, duplicate , compliance deadline missed, sync failure, Tally sync error Feature & content — release notes, new style feature release nudges, seasonal greetings via AI Send Greetings , compliance deadline calendar Each trigger carried execution context : legal requirement yes/no , average revenue at risk ₹ , and a P0–P3 priority. The full trigger matrix what we actually shipped Bucket Trigger Priority Channel Geo gated Revenue at risk Renewal D 30 renewal reminder P2 Push + Email All ₹500–5,000/user Renewal D 7 renewal reminder P1 Push + Email All ₹500–5,000/user Renewal D 1 renewal reminder P0 Push + SMS + Email All ₹500–5,000/user Renewal Trial expiry D 3 P1 Push + Email All ₹0 conversion Billing Invoice ready P1 Push All ₹100–10,000 Billing Payment failed P0 Push + SMS All ₹500–50,000 Billing Auto renewal confirmed P3 Push All — Transactional GST return filed P2 Push All — Transactional Payment received P2 Push All — Transactional Reversal confirmed P3 Push All — Transactional Credit note issued P3 Push All — Conflict GST rejection wrong GSTIN P0 Push + SMS All ₹10,000+ penalty Conflict GST rejection mismatch P0 Push + SMS All ₹10,000+ penalty Conflict GST rejection duplicate P1 Push All ₹5,000+ penalty Conflict Compliance deadline missed P0 Push + SMS All ₹25,000+ penalty Conflict Tally sync error P1 Push All Data integrity Conflict Bank reconciliation mismatch P1 Push All — Feature Release notes major P3 Push All — Feature New feature nudge P3 Push All — Feature Seasonal greeting P3 Push Geo 5 regions — Feature Compliance calendar alert P2 Push Geo 5 regions ₹10,000+ penalty Feature Year end checklist P2 Push All — Feature Quarterly audit reminder P2 Push All — System App update available P3 Push All — System Session expiry warning P1 Push All — The three rules that made it work 1. Priority tiers P0–P3 . The tiers rank what can interrupt vs what may wait. Billing and compliance errors are P0; a "new report is ready" ping is P3. Tier Definition Max latency Channels Example P0 Legal requirement, revenue at risk, user harm under 5 min Push + SMS + Email Payment failed, GST rejection P1 User action required, revenue impact under 30 min Push + Email Invoice ready, sync error P2 Helpful context, time sensitive under 4 hours Push Renewal D 7, GST filed P3 Nice to know, no urgency Next slot Push Release notes, greetings 2. Three slot daily cap. Only three notifications per user per day, globally. When the message isn't same day critical, it queues for tomorrow. Stacking is the single fastest way to get blocked and muted . The cap logic: 3. Geo segmented festivals. India sends greetings relevant pushes across five regional festival calendars rather than one national blast — relevance over reach. The conflict resolution logic the hard part When a P0 GST rejection and a P3 feature nudge collide on the same day for the same user, who wins? We built a conflict resolver that runs at send time: This resolver runs for every user, every send window. It's the reason engagement held. The technical architecture how it actually runs The notification system isn't a monolith — it's three services talking via a message queue: Trigger Service — Stateless Go service that evaluates 27+ triggers on schedule cron or event webhook . Each trigger is a small function: checkRenewalD7 , checkGSTRejection , etc. Outputs a normalized NotificationIntent to Kafka. Conflict Resolver — Consumer group that reads NotificationIntent , loads user state from Redis region, tier, opt outs, daily_sent_count , runs the resolver logic, outputs NotificationJob to delivery queue. Delivery Workers — Pool of workers that handle the actual send: FCM https://firebase.google.com/docs/cloud messaging for Android push Firebase Cloud Messaging APNs https://developer.apple.com/documentation/usernotifications for iOS push Apple Push Notification service Twilio for SMS P0 only SendGrid for email fallback Each worker has its own retry logic with exponential backoff. Failed deliveries go to a dead letter queue for manual review. The A/B tests that shaped the rules We didn't guess the cap or the tiers. We tested: Test Variant A Variant B Winner Lift Daily cap 5 slots 3 slots 3 slots +18% engagement P0 channels Push only Push+SMS+Email Push+SMS+Email +34% P0 open Geo gating National 5 regions 5 regions +42% festival engagement Cap enforcement Soft warn Hard defer Hard defer 67% opt outs The 3 slot cap was the single biggest win. At 5 slots, users started muting. At 3, engagement per send held steady for 6 months. The preference center what we should've built in month 1 Users wanted control. We added a preference center in month 3: The center itself is a simple React page backed by a Firestore document. The Conflict Resolver reads this before sending. Opt out rate dropped from 12% to under 2% within two weeks of launch. What the numbers said Metric Value Triggers mapped & released 27+ Priority tiers P0–P3 consistently honored Daily cap 3 slots per user Geo regions 5 festival calendars Engagement per send held no decay Opt out rate under 2% vs 12% pre cap Revenue recovered P0 billing ₹2.3M/quarter The engagement lift from the AI seasonal feature — +168% in the Send Greetings work /case studies/livekeeping send greetings — only works because users never felt spammed in the weeks before. What I'd do differently Instrument conflict logic first. We shipped conflict resolution rules last; measuring how many bad sends the resolver prevented would have justified the whole system in week one. Dry run the calendar. A festival calendar looks clean on paper; a dry run week would have caught the collisions with quiet hours and regional weekends before real users did. Build the preference center earlier. Users wanted to tune "I don't want payment received pings." We added it in month 3; should've been month 1. The constraint is the feature. Volume without a cap isn't a strategy — it's spam with a roadmap. I documented the complete trigger matrix in the push notification case study /case studies/livekeeping notifications . The seasonal greeting triggers it gates are the subject of the AI Send Greetings story /blog/ai send greetings 168 , and the same diagnose the workflow discipline is in the e invoice adoption gap /blog/e invoice adoption gap .

## Category page redesign that added +34% qualified leads

URL: https://saswatasg.com/blog/category-page-redesign-plus34

Story-led category journeys beat commodity grids: +17% PDP clicks, +34% qualified leads, −16% bounce in a 4-week sprint at Sierra.

Category pages look like static shelves; the data showed they were a two step conversation. At Sierra we replaced commodity grids with story driven journeys in a 4 week sprint, backed by GA4 custom events and Clarity heatmaps. Session to PDP click +17%, qualified leads +34%, bounce −16%, ATC +27% — on 1.1M BigQuery events, same traffic. Every category page in e commerce is a "am I in the right store?" moment. Most stores treat them as static shelves and leave the visitor to figure out intent alone. The data said something more interesting: the click happened, the click did nothing. The moment I stopped counting clicks The store's category pages got traffic. The products under them didn't get visits. It took exactly two weeks of GA4 custom events and Clarity scroll maps to see it — but once we had: Custom GA4 events — session start, category view, PDP click, ATC, form start. Microsoft Clarity https://clarity.microsoft.com/ heatmaps + scroll depth on every category template. The "quiet insight" turned out to be not quiet at all. Category clicks were big, but PDP engagement after the click was weak . Visitors clicked through a grid, landed on a product, and bounced off the page almost immediately. The funnel wasn't broken at the top — the storytelling was the leak. What the session tapes actually showed We watched 40+ category sessions back to back. The pattern was consistent: A visitor clicked a product from the grid. The product page loaded a bare spec table: dimensions, materials, price. The visitor looked for why this fits my space , didn't find it, and backed out within seconds. The store was selling furniture without saying who it's for . The redesign became a single question: how do we tell the visitor which product belongs to their life before they have to ask? The category page system we shipped Each redesigned module balanced four layers, in order of importance: 1. A guiding first section — why choose this category was layout, not a paragraph. The answer to "is this for me" appeared in the first screen. 2. Trust signals up top — guarantees, shipping windows, live ratings near first glance, not buried at the footer. 3. Intent filter scaffolding — the user narrows by aspiration "feed a family of 6" not by schema variables "seats: 6" . People don't search dining tables by attribute; they search by occasion. 4. Editorial PDP traction — the grid became teasers. Each cell teased the product story instead of a static image. How we measured it This was the part I'd defend most. We didn't launch "the new design" — each module shipped under a controlled rollout , with week over week comparisons against the same traffic baseline. If a module didn't move its KPI, it didn't stay. Three things made the measurement honest: 1. A fixed baseline. 1.1 million BigQuery events across the category templates, frozen before the first module shipped. No cherry picked week, no "one lucky day." 2. Same traffic, no ad changes. The budget didn't move. Any delta in behavior is behavior, not spend. 3. KPI at the cadence of decision. We watched the same five metrics for however long a change took to become boring — bounce, PDP click, ATC, qualified lead, session dwell. The week by week of a 4 week sprint Week 1 — instrument and freeze. GA4 events + Clarity heatmaps go live on every category template. Zero design decisions until the first read of where people stop. Week 2 — build story first, grid second. The leading question section, trust signals, and intent filters ship to one storefront category. Week 3 — iterate against the tape. Compare that one category against the baseline; keep or kill the modules. Week 4 — extend, then hold. Roll the winning modules across the other templates and freeze again. The discipline that got us to +34% qualified leads wasn't a bolder design. It was refusing to ship "the new design" without a control group. The numbers Metric Δ Session→PDP click +17% Qualified leads +34% Bounce rate −16% Add to cart rate +27% Events analyzed 1.1M BigQuery Qualified leads mattered more than raw traffic to the business — the store's lead form feeds its sales floor, so +34% qualified meant +34% on the pipeline, not +34% on a vanity count. That same form gets its own teardown in the +124% lead form fix /blog/lead form overhaul 124 . What I'd do differently Ship the editorial layer first. The story section drove more than the grid styling. In hindsight the order of builds was backwards — story before structure would've compounded the wins faster. Bank more session to PDP variants. We had one strong winner. A second iteration would've told us whether the win was the story or the trust signals, and run sooner. If your category pages don't convert, start here Adapt the exact recipe, sized to your store: 1. Instrument for two weeks before you design. GA4 events for category view → PDP click → ATC → lead; Clarity scroll + click maps. Freeze the baseline. 2. Answer "who is this for" on the first screen. Not with copy — with layout. One leading section, trust signals guarantee, shipping window, rating above the fold. 3. Replace attribute filters with intent filters. People don't search dining tables by "seat count"; they search by occasion. Offer "feed a family of six," not "seats: 6." 4. Make the grid a teaser. Each cell should hint the product story — why it fits a space — so the PDP click leads somewhere. Then ride one category for two weeks against your frozen baseline before touching the rest. If the module doesn't move all five KPIs, it doesn't ship everywhere. The tell a good category page has You know a category page is doing its job when a visitor can answer three questions without scrolling much: Is this store for me? Is this product for my space? What happens if I proceed? The old grids answered none of the three and blamed traffic. The redesigned modules answered one within the first viewport — which is why bounce fell 16 points and qualified leads rose 34. That's the whole principle, compressed: a category page is not a shelf. It's a first conversation. Baymard's e commerce UX research https://baymard.com/research makes the same case with 130,000+ hours of testing behind it. This is the deepest writeup in the category discovery case study /case studies/category discovery . Paired with the checkout teardown /blog/checkout abandonment 73 to 54 it's the funnel work that finally made the store's numbers explain themselves.
